Conference on Countering Terrorism Romania - Ministry of Foreign Affairs Type: Press release Date: 07/16/26 During her visit to the United States, Romania's Minister of Foreign Affairs, Oana Țoiu, participated in ceremonies marking the presence of the Romanian training ship Mircea in the United States as part of the events commemorating the 250th anniversary of the adoption of the U.S. Declaration of Independence. She also met with Romanian students studying at Harvard University. The visit included hosting a roundtable discussion at the Atlantic Council focused on the next steps following the NATO Summit in Ankara, as well as on Romania-U.S. cooperation in the fields of economic development and security. The Minister of Foreign Affairs held meetings with Members of the U.S. Congress, including Senator Steve Daines, Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee on Europe; Representatives Mike Rogers and Pat Harrington, Chairman and Member, respectively, of the House Armed Services Committee; Representative Joe Wilson, Co-Chair of the U.S. Helsinki Commission; Representative Gregory Meeks of New York; and Representative Kevin Self of Texas. Discussions focused on the outcomes of the NATO Summit, the presence of U.S. troops in Romania, increasing bilateral investment and economic partnerships, and strengthening cooperation between Romanian and American companies. This autumn, Romania will host for the first time the Romania-United States Exchange Program, welcoming a delegation of congressional staff and representatives of leading U.S. think tanks. The program follows the agreement concluded this spring between the Romanian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the U.S. Department of State. On 16 July, Minister Oana Țoiu will participate in the Ministerial Conference on the Resurgence of Political Terrorism, at the invitation of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. During the conference, she will present historical examples from Romania's experience in which political violence was used as an instrument by totalitarian regimes. Romania's painful experience with political repression, imprisonment, and state-sponsored crimes reinforces its commitment today to an agenda focused on prevention—addressing the conditions that enable political violence to take root, regardless of the ideology that seeks to legitimize violence as a political tool. The Minister will also present the European Union's perspective, drawing on the ProtectEU: European Internal Security Strategy, highlighting the need to strengthen efforts to prevent the online radicalization of young people and to enhance cooperation in preventing and countering terrorism.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text: The number of fostering households in England has dropped 10% since 2021, with over one in three foster carers now aged 60 or over. Photograph: Andor Bujdoso/Alamy View image in fullscreen The number of fostering households in England has dropped 10% since 2021, with over one in three foster carers now aged 60 or over. Photograph: Andor Bujdoso/Alamy Fostering Fostering in crisis: can flexible care models fix England’s child placement shortfall? New recruitment campaign to target adults in their 30s and 40s in bid to create 10,000 new foster care places Jessica Murray Social affairs correspondent Tue 13 Oct 2026 19.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Viennetta Basterfield, 67, spent two decades fostering more than 100 children in her west London home before she and her husband handed in the reins during Covid. Her own mother had died when she was nine and she was brought up by another woman who took her in. There was no doubt in her mind that she wanted to dedicate her life to passing that gift on to others. “I can’t say I wasn’t frightened. Every single placement I was frightened because you think, are we going to be OK? Are they going to accept us?” she said. “But it was the most rewarding thing I’ve ever done. We still have a full house for Sunday dinners, for christmas, for birthdays. “The greatest gift you can give a child is to show them that they matter.” But she worries about the future of fostering – she said the bureaucracy around the process was putting people off, and younger generations had more reservations about doing it, especially juggling it with caring for their own children. On Wednesday, the government is launching the country’s first national foster carer recruitment campaign, due to declining numbers at a time when there is a growing number of children in care. The number of fostering households has dropped 10% since 2021, and the foster care population is ageing, with over one in three foster carers now aged 60 or over. The appeal will target adults in their 30s and 40s, urging them “to open their hearts and homes to some of the most vulnerable children in society”, with the aim of creating 10,000 new foster care places by the end of this parliament. It will run alongside trials of new foster care models, such as short-term “respite fostering” or fostering at weekends, which the government hopes will make it accessible to a wider range of people. The children’s minister, Josh MacAlister, said he wanted the public to respond to the campaign in the same way many did to the Homes for Ukraine scheme, when hundreds opened their homes to refugees. “There was this massive national moment where we understood that something was happening and people asked themselves, could we help? We need that kind of moment, to prompt people to have conversations in their homes,” he said. “Lots of families won’t be able to do it, but we’re trying to open up fostering to a wider group of people, by making it intergenerational or part-time, for instance.” He urged families not to wait for the “perfect moment”. “You’ve already got a lot of what it takes. Just step forward and start the process and see where you go,” he said. “Unless we rapidly, dramatically expand the foster care system, we will end up with children waking up every single day in residential care who could be in a family home, and children who are sent to live miles away from where they’ve grown up.” Speaking at an event ahead of the campagin at Downing Street on Tuesday, Marie-France van Heel, the prime minister’s wife, revealed for the first time that she had wanted to foster children. She was put off the idea because of her husband’s job and feeling she had to “transform myself into a different type of person to be able to give foster care”. “This campaign is really trying to dispel some of those myths and misconceptions,” she said. Fostering is the primary form of care for looked-after children in England. Out of 81,770 looked-after children, there are about 56,400 children in foster care at any one time. New research by the Coram Institute for Children found over half a million adults want to foster and an estimated 3.4 million are interested. Dame Carol Homden, CEO of Coram, said there was a “substantial pool of people who are open to becoming foster carers” and the charity welcomed the government’s ambitious plans to recruit more. Their research has identified certain groups with a higher fostering propensity who could be targeted, including women, larger households and those from minoritised ethnic backgrounds, particularly black households. But there also needs to be a focus on retaining current foster carers as well as recruiting new ones, Homden said. Research has shown a number of factors are pushing foster carers to leave the sector, including feeling undervalued or ignored by social workers, and financial strain – the Fostering Network found only 33% of carers report their allowances fully cover the cost of raising a child . “We need to see a focus on targeting key areas and groups, clear information and practical support to boost both recruitment and retention of foster carers,” said Homden. Polling by the Department for Education found that two-thirds (66%) of people believe they could be a good foster carer if practical barriers were removed. https://townhall.com/columnists/michaelb.text: The Vanishing Myth of the Gaza Genocide Michael Brown Oct 09, 2026 12:01 AM Oct 09, 2026 Opinion The opinions expressed by columnists are their own and do not necessarily represent the views of Townhall.com. Advertisement AP Photo/Jehad Alshrafi I write these words from Poland, where 90 percent of Poland’s Jews — 3 million out of 3.3 million — were slaughtered during World War II. That is what genocide looks like. In stark contrast, roughly 70,000 of Gaza’s 2.3 million residents were killed during Israel’s war with Hamas, amounting to approximately 3 percent of the population. And that figure includes enemy combatants. Yet the same word, genocide, used for the systematic, intentional murder of 90 percent of Poland’s Jews — and two-thirds of Europe’s Jews as a whole — is being used to describe Israel’s war with Hamas. How can this be? And where is the moral equivalence? Advertisement Recently, more than 6,000 public figures signed an open letter denouncing the Gaza genocide libel, and while the acute suffering of the people of Gaza must not be minimized, these public figures are correct: it is grossly inaccurate and even immoral to label their suffering a “genocide.” This does not mean that the IDF always acted justly and morally or that several prominent Israeli leaders have not made inexcusable statements. Nor does debunking the genocide lie minimize the very real and acute suffering of the Gazan population. A tragic death is a tragic death. But tragic deaths in war do not equate with a genocide. Consider first the numbers involved. The Holocaust killed 6 million of Europe’s 9 million Jews (67 percent); in Poland, 90 percent of Jews were murdered. The Armenian genocide (1915–1916) killed 664,000–1.2 million of roughly 1.5 million Armenians (44–80 percent). The Rwandan genocide (1994) killed 500,000–1 million people, overwhelmingly Tutsi, in just 100 days, out of roughly 1 million Tutsi in Rwanda. Under the Khmer Rouge (1975–1979), nearly 2 million Cambodians died — roughly 25–30 percent of the country’s population. Israel’s war with Hamas resulted in the deaths of approximately 70,000 people, representing three percent of the population. How can this possibly be referred to as a “genocide”? We are often told that the answer is “intent,” the allegation is that it was the intent of the IDF (and/or the Israeli government) to wipe out the Gazan population, just as the Nazis planned to wipe out Europe’s Jews. Recommended Dem Hack Drops the Mask and Lets Her Fascism Freak Flag Fly Kurt Schlichter Illegal Alien Reportedly Arrested for Beheading Iwo Jima Monument in Virginia Scott McClallen Advertisement This, too, is categorically false. To the contrary, Israel took extraordinary measures to minimize civilian casualties, despite Hamas embedding itself in the civilian population and Hamas combatants wearing civilian clothing. Just two months into the war (as of December 8, 2023), the IDF had made more than 12 million prerecorded phone calls, sent out more than 15 million texts, dropped more than 4.5 million leaflets, and placed more than 45,000 individual calls, “warning civilians to evacuate areas of hostilities and individual targets.” What other nation has ever made such efforts to spare civilian lives in the midst of a brutal war? This is the opposite of genocidal intent. As for the charge of starvation, according to Israel’s Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories , more than 1 million metric tons of food entered Gaza between October 7, 2023, and January 17, 2025 alone. Based on the actual composition of the food entering Gaza, this represented roughly 2,600 calories per person per day. This does not mean that all the food actually reached the people, as there were massive distribution issues. But when it comes to intent, if you’re trying to wipe out a people group, you don’t make every effort to give them time to evacuate before bombing, nor do you send them food if you’re trying to starve them to death. Advertisement All this is underscored by the fact that as many as 81 percent of the structures in Gaza were damaged or destroyed in the war, yet only 3 percent of the people were killed. And according to the IDF, at least 25,000 of those killed were Hamas combatants. There is also the issue of outright propaganda, with charges of “genocide” and “starvation” circulating before the Israeli offensive had even begun. As documented by NGO Monitor , on October 9, 2023, just two days after the massacre, Al-Haq, Al Mezan and the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights accused Israel of “employing starvation as a weapon.” On October 11, Al-Haq said Israeli actions amounted to “acts of genocide.” By October 15, the three groups were calling on states to protect Palestinians “against genocide”—still two weeks before the IDF’s ground invasion. Yet there’s more. Israel’s critics have raised the genocide charge against the Jewish state for decades, during which time the Palestinian population in Gaza and the West Bank has grown dramatically. In 2001, the Durban World Conference Against Racism NGO declaration called for investigation and prosecution of alleged “war crimes, acts of genocide and ethnic cleansing” by Israel. In 2008–09, UN General Assembly President Miguel d'Escoto Brockmann publicly said Israel's actions raised the issue of genocide. In 2014, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas accused Israel at the UN of conducting a “war of genocide” against Palestinians in Gaza. Advertisement Contrast all this rhetoric with the fact that in 1967, when Israel took control of Gaza, the population was between 400,000–440,000. Immediately before October 7, 2023, the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics estimated 2,226,544 residents. This means that Gaza's Palestinian population had grown by 400–450 percent — all while Israel was committing “genocide” against the people of Gaza! As for the West Bank, prior to the 1967 war, the population was estimated at 850,000. By 2023, PCBS estimated the population at 3,256,906 — approximately a fourfold increase, or an increase of about 280 percent. Where was the genocide? Lastly, it has recently been revealed that, according to evidence released by the IDF, 170 Palestinians presented as journalists killed during the war were also operatives in Hamas, Islamic Jihad, or other terrorist organizations, while other Palestinian journalists have openly described Hamas intimidation , interference with content, threats, and resulting self-censorship. In sum: 1) the number of deaths says there was no genocide; 2) there was no intent to commit genocide (quite the contrary); 3) the charge of genocide was used as a propaganda weapon before the war even began, not to mention in previous decades; and 4) much of the reporting from within Gaza was extremely biased, if not completely propagandistic. Advertisement If the IDF committed war crimes, those must be investigated. The extremist voices within Israel must be countered. And the people of Gaza deserve compassion, with a path for a potentially better life. But, to say it once more, there was no genocide in Gaza. Enough with this perfidious lie.
